stories.headline: Why there has never been any lead in a pencil
stories.summary: The black core of a pencil is graphite and has never contained the element lead. A large deposit of graphite was discovered at Borrowdale in Cumbria in 1565; in 1795 Nicolas-Jacques Conté found a way to mix powdered graphite with clay and fire it, and in 1858 Hymen Lipman patented the pencil with an eraser on the end.

stories.headline: Every tile in the box: the arithmetic of a domino set
stories.summary: The traditional European domino set has 28 tiles, showing every combination of spot counts from zero to six. Larger sets extend the idea: a double-nine set has 55 tiles, a double-twelve set 91.

stories.headline: The hill where the world's clocks are set
stories.summary: The Royal Observatory, Greenwich, stands on a hill in Greenwich Park in south-east London, overlooking the Thames. Commissioned by Charles II in 1675, it gave its name to Greenwich Mean Time after the 1884 International Meridian Conference in Washington chose the meridian through it as the world's prime meridian.

payload.dispatch: The black core of a pencil is graphite, not lead, and has never contained the element lead. A large deposit of graphite was discovered at Borrowdale in Cumbria, England, in 1765. In 1795 Nicolas-Jacques Conté found a way to mix powdered graphite with clay and fire the rods in a kiln, and on 30 March 1858 Hymen Lipman received the first patent for attaching an eraser to the end of a pencil.

evidence.title: Borrowdale
evidence.text: In 1565 (some sources say as early as 1500), a large deposit of graphite was discovered on the approach to Grey Knotts from the hamlet of Seathwaite in Borrowdale parish, Cumbria, England.

evidence.title: Clay, kilns and erasers
evidence.text: In 1795, Nicolas-Jacques Conté discovered a method of mixing powdered graphite with clay and forming the mixture into rods that were then fired in a kiln. On 30 March 1858, Hymen Lipman received the first patent for attaching an eraser to the end of a pencil.

reveal.explanation: The Borrowdale graphite was found in 1565, two centuries before the dispatch's date. Conté's clay process of 1795 and Lipman's eraser patent of 30 March 1858 are correct.

sources.excerpt: The black core of pencils is still referred to as lead, even though it never contained the element lead. In 1565 (some sources say as early as 1500), a large deposit of graphite was discovered on the approach to Grey Knotts from the hamlet of Seathwaite in Borrowdale parish, Cumbria, England. In 1795, Nicolas-Jacques Conté discovered a method of mixing powdered graphite with clay and forming the mixture into rods that were then fired in a kiln. On 30 March 1858, Hymen Lipman received the first patent for attaching an eraser to the end of a pencil.

payload.question: How many tiles are in a traditional double-six domino set?
payload.comparison: A double-nine set, the next size up, has 55 tiles.

reveal.context: The traditional European domino set consists of 28 tiles, featuring all combinations of spot counts between zero and six. The common extended sets are double-nine (55 tiles), double-twelve (91 tiles), double-fifteen (136 tiles) and double-eighteen (190 tiles).

sources.excerpt: The traditional European domino set consists of 28 tiles, also known as pieces, bones, rocks, stones, men, cards or just dominoes, featuring all combinations of spot counts between zero and six. The common extended sets are double-nine (55 tiles), double-12 (91 tiles), double-15 (136 tiles), and double-18 (190 tiles), which is the maximum in practice.

clues: An observatory commissioned by a king in 1675 stands on a hill in a park, overlooking a river to the north.
In 1884 a conference in Washington chose the meridian passing through it as the prime meridian for the whole world, and it gave its name to a time standard.

reveal.explanation: The Royal Observatory, Greenwich, is situated on a hill in Greenwich Park in south-east London, overlooking the River Thames to the north. It was commissioned in 1675 by King Charles II. In 1884 the International Meridian Conference in Washington decided that the Greenwich meridian should be the prime meridian for the whole world, and the observatory gave its name to Greenwich Mean Time.

sources.excerpt: The Royal Observatory, Greenwich (51°28′37″N 0°00′53″W) is an observatory situated on a hill in Greenwich Park in south east London, overlooking the River Thames to the north. Because the Prime Meridian passed through it, it gave its name to Greenwich Mean Time. The observatory was commissioned in 1675 by King Charles II. In 1884 the International Meridian Conference in Washington D.C. decided that the Greenwich Prime Meridian should be the Prime meridian for the whole world.
